info.title: keyext.server
info.description:
A headless JSON-RPC interface to the KeY theorem prover, for automated agents.

One rule governs everything here: the only legitimate source of 'this is verified' is KeY's own Proof.closed(), reported as Statistics.closed. No error path, no timeout, no task reaching SUCCEEDED may be read as a closed proof. A task that finished is a task that finished.

Transport: POST /rpc for calls, GET /rpc for a Server-Sent Events stream carrying task.progress and task.finished as JSON-RPC notifications. Bound to 127.0.0.1 only; there is no authentication, so reach a remote instance through an SSH tunnel.

Third-party tool, not an official KeY component.

methods.name: task.cancel
methods.summary: Ask a task to stop.
methods.description: Reports whether the request was passed on, not that the task has stopped: KeY notices between rule applications. Poll until the status reaches CANCELLED.

methods.name: proof.save
methods.summary: Write a proof to disk in KeY's own format.
methods.description: Until a proof is written out it lives only as long as this server, which makes every result unreviewable: there is nothing to read, re-check or commit. The format is KeY's, so the file can be loaded by KeY itself and not only by this server.

params.name: proof
params.description: The proof to write out. It does not have to be closed; a partial proof is saved as it stands and reloads to the same partial state.

params.name: path
params.description: Relative paths are taken against the workspace. When omitted the proof is named after itself, in the workspace.

params.name: asBundle
params.description: Write a .zproof bundle carrying the sources, not a bare .proof.

result.name: saved
result.description: Where the proof was written and how large the file is.

errors.message: PROOF_NOT_FOUND — the proof identifier is unknown or the proof was disposed of
SAVE_FAILED — the proof was not written. KeY's saver reports its failures by returning them rather than throwing, so this code exists to make sure one is never mistaken for a path

methods.name: proof.loadFile
methods.summary: Replay a saved proof into an environment of its own.
methods.description: The other half of proof.save. A file that replays only in part is refused rather than served: the resulting proof looks like any other from the outside, and the steps that are missing are exactly the ones that failed.

params.name: path
params.description: A .proof or .zproof file. Its environment is loaded first and is returned alongside the proof; a proof whose steps could not all be replayed is an error rather than a partially replayed proof.

result.name: task
result.description: A handle on the task doing the loading and the replay. Poll task.get; its result carries the environment that was loaded and the replayed proof. A proof whose steps could not all be replayed fails the task rather than arriving partially replayed.

methods.name: proof.prune
methods.summary: Cut a proof back to a node, discarding everything below it.
methods.description: How to take back a wrong turn without starting the proof again from the contract. Refused when it would remove nothing, when the proof is closed (KeY's own default), and when a merge rule was applied below the node — undoing one of those reaches its partners on a thread this server does not control.

params.name: proof
params.description: The proof to cut back.

params.name: nodeId
params.description: The node to cut back to, as reported by goal.list.

result.name: pruned
result.description: The goal the proof was cut back to, how many nodes went away, and what the proof looks like now.

GOAL_NOT_FOUND — the proof has no node with that number

INVALID_PARAMS — the parameters did not fit, or there was nothing to prune at that node: it is already an open goal, it is closed and KeY declines to prune closed proofs, or a merge rule was applied below it

EnvironmentRef.description: Opaque handle on a loaded project. Pass it back as received; never build one.

proofId.description: Identifier of a proof held open by this instance.

GoalRef.description: Opaque handle on one goal of one proof. KeY numbers nodes per proof, so a goal has no identity outside its proof and the reference carries both halves.

proofId.description: The proof the goal belongs to.

goalId.description: The goal within that proof. Goal identifiers are the node numbers KeY assigns, and they move as a proof grows, so re-read them rather than keeping one across steps.

Ok.description: The request was carried out. Never a statement about a proof.

ok.description: Whether the request was carried out. It reports on the request and never on a proof: no value of this field means anything was proved. Most methods only ever answer true and report failure as an error; task.cancel also answers false, when there was nothing left to interrupt.

SourcePosition.description: A place in a source file KeY attached to a failure.

file.description: The file, as the environment resolved it.

message.description: What is at that position, in KeY's words.

ErrorData.description: Machine-readable detail on an error. Branch on the numeric code, never on message text.

positions.description: Places in the sources the error can be pinned to, when there are any. Parse and type errors carry these; a failure with no source location leaves the list empty.

detail.description: The underlying message, kept verbatim rather than reworded.

TaskKind.description: What a task is doing. It says which method started the work, not how the work turned out.

TaskStatus.description: SUCCEEDED means the work finished without throwing. It does NOT mean a proof closed. A macro that runs to its end leaving three goals open is a SUCCEEDED task with three open goals; only Statistics.closed answers the other question.

TaskHandle.description: The state of one long-running operation.

taskId.description: Identifier to poll with task.get and to pass to task.cancel.

kind.description: Which kind of work this task is running.

status.description: Where the task is. SUCCEEDED means the work ran to an end without throwing. It does NOT mean a proof closed; only Statistics.closed says that.

subject.description: What the task operates on: an EnvironmentRef or a ProofRef.

result.description: The product of a succeeded task.

error.description: Why the task FAILED. Absent otherwise.

envId.description: Identifier to state later calls against.

path.description: What was loaded, as an absolute path.

proofCount.description: How many proofs are currently open under this environment.

ProofObligationKind.description: INFORMATION_FLOW is only produced when a provider of KeY's InformationFlowContractSupplier is on the class path, which this build does not ship. OTHER is reported rather than guessing at a kind that might be wrong.

ProofObligation.description: One thing KeY can be asked to prove, derived from a specification.

contractId.description: KeY's unique internal contract name. Pass it to proof.start.

kind.description: What kind of obligation this is.

targetClass.description: Fully qualified name of the class it is about.

targetMember.description: Signature such as add(int, int); the parameter types distinguish overloads.

hasExistingProof.description: Whether a proof for this obligation is already open in this instance.

Statistics.description: What is known about a proof. `closed` is the only field that answers whether anything was verified, and it is read from KeY's own Proof.closed() every time this object is built: never cached, never defaulted, never inferred from a task having finished.

closed.description: Whether the proof is closed. This is KeY's own Proof.closed(), and it is the only field in this protocol that says a contract has been proved. No task status, no macro finishing and no absence of errors means the same thing.

openGoals.description: How many goals are still open. Zero exactly when closed is true.

interactiveSteps.description: Rule applications that came from a script or a macro rather than from the automatic search.

smtSolverApps.description: Goals discharged by an external SMT solver. These are closed on the solver's word, not by KeY's calculus.

autoModeTimeMs.description: Milliseconds spent in the automatic search.

AutoModeOutcome.description: Why the search stopped. None of these says anything about success. What they do say is whether more of the same would help: MAX_RULES, BUDGET_ELAPSED and STRATEGY_TIMEOUT mean the search was still working when it was stopped, while EXHAUSTED means the prover did everything it knows and the goals left need a script, a solver or a specification rather than more time.

AutoModeResult.description: The result member of a finished AUTO task.

proof.description: The proof the search ran on.

statistics.description: What the proof looks like now, including whether it closed.

ProofRunResult.description: The result member of a finished MACRO or SCRIPT task.

proof.description: The proof the work ran on.

statistics.description: What the proof looks like now, including whether it closed.

GoalSummary.description: goalId and nodeId are the same number today: KeY identifies a goal by the serial of the node it sits on. Both are reported because they are used in different places and a client should not have to know they coincide.

goal.description: Reference to pass to the methods that act on a goal.

goalId.description: The goal's identifier, the same number as in goal.

nodeId.description: The proof node this goal sits at. Pass it to proof.prune to cut back here.

isOpen.description: Whether the goal still needs work.

isLinked.description: Whether the goal is closed by a link to another part of the proof rather than by its own branch.

SequentFormat.description: TEXT is KeY's pretty-printed rendering, UNICODE the same with logical symbols, and STRUCTURED the same again with each formula also taken apart into its symbolic state, the program still to run, and what must hold once it has.

Sequent.description: The rendering of one goal's sequent.

antecedent.description: The formulas assumed, one rendered string each.

succedent.description: The formulas to be shown, one rendered string each. The goal holds if any one of them follows from all of the antecedent.

format.description: The format the strings were rendered in.

formulas.description: Present only for STRUCTURED. antecedent and succedent are present regardless.

Macro.description: One proof macro: a named, pre-packaged sequence of prover steps.

macroId.description: Also the macro's name inside a proof script.

name.description: The macro's name as KeY shows it.

category.description: How KeY groups the macro in its own menus.

description.description: What the macro does, in KeY's words.

StuckReason.description: NEEDS_SPEC is asked of KeY's own rule application - whether a loop invariant application found an invariant, whether a contract application found a contract - not inferred from the rule's type. Where that cannot be established the answer is NOT_INSTANTIABLE rather than a cause that might be wrong.

StuckPoint.description: A rule that KeY would like to apply to a goal and cannot.

ruleId.description: Stable identifier: the rule's implementation class name.

ruleName.description: The same rule as KeY displays it.

positionHint.description: Where in the goal it would have applied, in readable terms.

source.description: Where in the Java source this points, when it points anywhere.

GoalDiagnostics.description: An empty stuckPoints list is a finding, not a blank: no built-in rule applies here, so the goal is not waiting on a missing specification. Read it with lastSearchOutcome to tell a prover that ran out of ideas from one that ran out of budget.

goalId.description: The goal this entry is about.

stuckPoints.description: Where the search ran out of ways forward in this goal. An empty list does not mean the goal is fine: read lastSearchOutcome and truncated to tell 'nothing is missing' from 'the search never got that far'.

truncated.description: The probe reached its depth ceiling before the end of a formula.

lastSearchOutcome.description: How the last automatic search on this proof ended, absent when none has run. Read an empty stuckPoints list together with this: empty after EXHAUSTED means the prover tried and ran out of ideas, empty after a limit means it never finished looking. The two are the same list and opposite problems.

ServerVersion.description: The identity and capabilities of one running instance.

apiVersion.description: The protocol version, the same string this document is versioned with. Clients should check it.

keyVersion.description: The version of KeY doing the proving.

instanceId.description: Identifies this process, so a client can tell a restarted instance from the one it was talking to.

threads.description: How many prover threads the instance was started with. Fixed for its lifetime.

SavedProof.description: Where a proof was written. That this object exists at all means the file is on disk: a save that did not happen is reported as an error, never as a path.

path.description: Absolute path of the file that was written.

EnvironmentLoaded.description: What a finished LOAD or REPLAY task produced. A .proof or .zproof file brings a proof with it; the field is absent for a project or a problem file that declares none.

envId.description: Identifier of the environment that was loaded.

proof.description: The proof that came with the file, when a .proof or .zproof was loaded. Absent when sources were loaded.

SequentSide.description: Which side of the turnstile a formula sits on: assumed, or to be shown.

StructuredFormula.description: One formula taken apart. A proof obligation in mid-flight prints as a single formula several hundred characters long whose interesting part is the last thirty; separated, each piece answers a different question and can be read on its own. The split is KeY's own, taken from the position table it builds while printing, so it cannot drift from what KeY thinks the formula is.

side.description: Which side of the turnstile the formula is on.

index.description: Position within that side, matching the antecedent or succedent array.

state.description: The symbolic state (KeY's update). Absent when there is none.

program.description: The Java still to be executed. Absent when there is none.

claim.description: The formula with the state and the program elided, marked with an ellipsis: what remains to be shown about them. For a formula with neither, the whole formula.

RuleKind.description: How a taclet finds what it applies to. KeY's categorisation, not an assessment.

ApplicableRule.description: A rule that applies to a goal here and now, and how to write it down. `script` is the useful field: a rule name alone is often not enough, since a third to a half of the rules offered on a real goal match in more than one place and a script naming one without saying which is refused. The enumeration mirrors the `rule` script command's own, so the occurrence count reported is the count that command will find.

ruleId.description: The taclet's name, which is what a proof script's rule command takes.

kind.description: Whether the rule matches a formula and where. NO_FIND rules apply to a sequent as a whole; the rule command cannot apply them, so they come with no script.

side.description: Which side the first match is on. Absent for NO_FIND.

index.description: The formula the first match is under. Absent for NO_FIND.

needsInstantiation.description: Schema variables remain to be filled in, with inst_… in a script.

needsAssumption.description: The rule has an \assumes clause and no instantiation has been chosen.

occurrences.description: How many places the rule matches. Beyond the first they are reached by raising the occurrence number in `script`, which counts from zero.

script.description: The line to hand to goal.applyScript to apply the first match. Absent when the rule needs input this cannot supply — see needsInstantiation and needsAssumption.

GoalRules.description: What could still be applied to a goal by hand: the complement of stuck points. Those say what wants to apply and cannot; this says what could apply and the automatic strategy did not choose, which after a search that came back EXHAUSTED is what is left to look at. No judgement is offered about which are worth trying — cut and hide_left apply almost anywhere. Rules carrying a `script` can be applied as they stand; the rest are offered because they are genuinely applicable and a caller may know what to supply.

goalId.description: The goal these rules apply to.

rules.description: The rules that match, one entry per rule rather than per occurrence.

PrunedProof.description: What pruning removed. The count is reported because KeY answers "nothing to do" and "done" in ways that look alike from outside; a prune that would remove nothing is refused rather than reported here.

goal.description: The goal the proof was cut back to, now open again.

statistics.description: What the proof looks like after pruning. Pruning an open proof cannot close it, and pruning a closed one opens it.

server.name: server
server.description: The instance itself: what it is, whether it is answering, what it can do, and how to stop it. None of these methods touch a proof.

environment.name: environment
environment.description: Loading Java sources and their specifications, and listing the proof obligations that come out of them. An environment owns the class types and the contracts every proof under it is stated against.

proof.name: proof
proof.description: The lifetime of a single proof attempt: starting one from a contract, running the automatic search, asking what it has achieved, undoing part of it, and writing it to disk.

goal.name: goal
goal.description: Working on the open goals of a proof: reading a sequent, and driving the prover at a goal by hand with a macro or a proof script.

diagnostics.name: diagnostics
diagnostics.description: Answering why a proof did not close. These methods only observe; none of them changes a proof.

task.name: task
task.description: The asynchronous work anything long-running is handed off to. A task finishing reports that the work ran to an end, and nothing about the proof it ran on.

externalDocs.description: The KeY prover this server embeds: its calculus, its specification language, and how to read the sequents these methods return.
